name: Beth Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, of course. I actually like this sort of thing. I filled in the last staff survey with three pages of comments, and I don't think anyone read it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the packaging end of a biscuit factory, line four. The biscuits come out of the oven and cool on a long belt, and my machines wrap them, box them and stack the boxes, with two small robots, cobots we call them, that work next to us and do the stacking. I run the wrapper settings, change the film reels, sort out jams and watch the check-weigher, the scale that throws out packs that are too light. I start at two in the afternoon and finish at ten. The smell of the ovens is the best part, I still like it after nine years, and the worst part is when the film tears five times in an hour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the cobots. How do you get on with them?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine, honestly. I was the one who learned how to reteach their stacking pattern when we changed box sizes, because nobody else wanted to. I also use an AI chat tool every day, on my phone, to look up error codes and to write our handover notes so the night shift can actually read them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a lot of fuss for some better spellcheck. At work I'd joke that the cobots keep their jobs and so do we. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should have gone into wages instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be a bit let down. I like the tools, they make my shift easier, and I'd hoped they'd make the boring parts of the job go away. But for the family it's fine, everything stays as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. I'd still use the chat tool for error codes, and I'd keep pushing to get on the engineering team's training for the cobots. Marco and I would carry on with the house plan, maybe a loft room in a year or two, we've got the savings for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little bit of 'is that it?'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still push for that training if nothing big was changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I'd still want to learn the cobot programming properly, because that's interesting work and it pays better. I'd just do it for me, not because I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to hear from about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union, I think. If the bosses are already saving an hour a shift with these tools, I want that hour back as pay, not as a smaller team. Small gains still count.

S0.say: That's a lot of fuss for some better spellcheck. I'd joke at work that the cobots keep their jobs and so do we, and online I'd say the money should have gone into wages.
S0.think: I'd be a bit let down, because the tools make my shift easier and I'd hoped they'd take away the boring parts. For the family, though, everything staying the same is fine.
S0.do: Keeps using the chat tool for error codes and keeps pushing for the engineering team's cobot training. Goes ahead with a loft room in a year or two using savings.
S0.feel: Calm, with a little bit of 'is that it?'
S0.quote: If the bosses are already saving an hour a shift with these tools, I want that hour back as pay, not as a smaller team.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is the rare operator who's disappointed that AI might fizzle. She already uses AI daily and reteaches the cobots, so she sees tools as a way up. Even in a quiet future she frames time savings as something workers should get back through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be good for us if we organise. Get the union to bargain for training and a share of the savings, and make sure the people on the line are the first ones offered the new jobs, not people from outside. I'd post that in our shift chat and probably bore everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of it. I'm already the one who fixes the cobots, so I'd be the obvious person to move up into running them. I'd worry more about my friends on the line than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the automation technician course straight away, the one the college runs on Saturdays, and ask the company to pay half. I'd start using the AI tool to study the robot manuals in the evenings. And I'd go to the union meeting and ask to be on whatever group negotiates the changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit excited, actually. And a bit guilty about being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Dee, who's worked next to me for nine years, can't read the screens without her glasses and won't ask for help. If line four gets two more cobots, I'm the one who gets a better job and Dee's the one who gets moved to nights. That doesn't sit right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for Dee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make her come to the study sessions with me, honestly. I'd set up a little group in the canteen on Thursdays. It's what I'd want someone to do for me.

S1.say: This could be good for us if we organise: training, a share of the savings and first pick of the new jobs for people already on the line. I'd post that in our shift chat and probably bore everyone.
S1.think: I think I'd do well out of it, since I'm already the one who fixes the cobots. I'd worry more about my friends on the line than about me.
S1.do: Signs up straight away for the Saturday automation technician course and asks the company to pay half. Studies robot manuals with AI in the evenings, joins the union's negotiating group and sets up a Thursday study group.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a bit excited, with some guilt about being excited.
S1.quote: If line four gets two more cobots, I'm the one who gets a better job and Dee's the one who gets moved to nights.
S1.fieldNote: Beth expects to gain from steady change and says so, then immediately turns to who loses. Her guilt about Dee is the honest heart of this scenario. Her progressive views show up as practical organising, not slogans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a proper public response: a basic income, a tax on automated output, free retraining. I'd go to marches and write to my representative, which I've done before about the hospital closure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd realise my cobot skills only buy me a year or two. If AI can do almost anything, it can program a stacking pattern better than me. I'd be one of the last on the line, but still on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay and make myself useful as long as possible, running the changeover to the new robots, because whoever does that gets kept on longest. I'd move some of our savings into a fund that holds robot and AI companies, maybe 10,000, so at least we own a slice of what's replacing us. And I'd get stuck into the campaigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because we've got savings and Marco's teaching job, but I'd be on my phone at midnight reading everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, and what doesn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is barely enough to learn one thing. I'd have to pick what I can learn in six months and use for eighteen. In two years you don't change careers, you just pick the last chair to sit on before the music stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Marco's teaching job be safe, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if everyone's losing jobs at the same time. So the shares and the politics are the backup.

S2.say: This is the moment for a proper public response: basic income, a tax on automated output and free retraining. I'd march and write to my representative like I did about the hospital closure.
S2.think: My cobot skills would only buy me a year or two, because AI could program a stacking pattern better than me. I'd be one of the last on the line, but still on the line.
S2.do: Stays and leads the changeover to new robots to be kept on longest. Moves about 10,000 of savings into a fund holding robot and AI companies, and throws herself into campaigning.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, thanks to savings and her husband's job, though she'd be reading on her phone at midnight.
S2.quote: In two years you don't change careers, you just pick the last chair to sit on before the music stops.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest scenario Beth looks for a role, choosing to run the changeover. She mixes left-leaning politics with buying shares in the robot makers and sees no contradiction. Her savings and Marco's job keep her from alarm, though she doubts teaching would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste the first two arguing about whether it's real. Start the training schemes and the income support now. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me a real path. I could finish the technician course, get onto the engineering team, maybe even move to a firm that installs these systems. It'd only last so long, but it's a lot better than two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the Saturday course in the first year and apply for the engineering team. If the company wouldn't move me, I'd look at the robot installation firms nearby, there are at least three in the business park. I'd put 300 a month into the robot fund too, rather than one big lump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. There's still an end point, but I've got time to get my feet under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still worry about the people around you, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With five years I'd still try to get Dee and the others into the study group. With two years I don't think I would have, I'd have been too busy saving myself. More time makes me a nicer person, which isn't something I like admitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're eleven and eight. I'd tell them to learn how things work, not just how to use them. Nina already takes apart the toaster, so we're halfway there.

S3.say: We've got five years, so let's not waste the first two arguing about whether it's real. Start the training schemes and income support now.
S3.think: Five years gives me a real path: finish the technician course, join the engineering team or move to an installer. It would only last so long, but it's far better than two years.
S3.do: Finishes the Saturday course in the first year and applies for the engineering team, or one of three robot installation firms in the business park. Puts 300 a month into a robot fund.
S3.feel: Uneasy, knowing there's an end point but with time to get her footing.
S3.quote: More time makes me a nicer person, which isn't something I like admitting.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Beth a career path she can name, including firms in the local business park. She admits that time makes her more generous, which is a striking piece of self-knowledge. Her kids' curiosity gives her some hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to do this fairly, if we decide to. Shorter working weeks, retraining for everyone, and a share of the gains going back to people. I'd be at the meetings making that case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd plan to be one of the people setting up and fixing these systems for most of that decade. After that, I don't know. I'd be fifty-three and I'd want there to be a decent public safety net, because I don't think any job is safe at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as five years but slower and more thought through. Finish the course, move to the engineering team, keep putting money into the fund, and pay off the mortgage by about 2034. I'd also run for the union committee, so I'm part of the deal, not just affected by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but quite hopeful. More hopeful than with the fast ones, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you'd do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be grabbing. With ten I can actually do it properly and bring people with me. Ten years is long enough to train Dee and short enough that we'd both still be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of 2036 worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat, quiet bit after. When there's nothing to fix. I'd want to still be useful to someone. Maybe volunteering, maybe teaching at the college, I don't know yet.

S4.say: A decade is enough to do this fairly if we decide to: shorter weeks, retraining for everyone and a share of the gains going back to people. I'd be at the meetings making that case.
S4.think: I'd plan to be setting up and fixing these systems for most of the decade. After that, at fifty-three, I'd want a decent public safety net, because I don't think any job is safe at the end.
S4.do: Finishes the course, moves to the engineering team and keeps investing in the robot fund. Aims to pay off the mortgage by about 2034 and runs for the union committee.
S4.feel: Uneasy but fairly hopeful, more than with the faster scenarios.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to train Dee and short enough that we'd both still be scared.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Beth do things 'properly and bring people with me'. Her worry shifts from income to purpose after there's nothing left to fix. She trusts a public safety net rather than her own savings to carry the end point.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to bring anyone with you. What would help is training that starts before the robots arrive, paid for by the companies, and some kind of income guarantee so people aren't choosing between rent and a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd miss. I'd miss the smell of the ovens more than the money, and nobody's going to put that in a spreadsheet.

headlineQuote: I'd miss the smell of the ovens more than the money, and nobody's going to put that in a spreadsheet.
portrait: Beth Rossi is 43 and runs the packaging end of a biscuit line, working beside two cobots she taught herself to reprogram, with a teacher husband and two children. She uses AI every day and is curious, organised and left-leaning, often thinking first of colleagues like Dee who'd be left behind. She stays calm and even excited about steady change, becomes anxious but active when AGI comes in two years, and with more time plans a path into robot engineering while campaigning for fair rules. Her savings and investments steady her, but she pins her long-term hopes on a public safety net.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time to bring anyone with her.
whatWouldHelp: Training that starts before the robots arrive, paid by the companies, plus an income guarantee so people don't have to choose between rent and a course.
